The Fed chair said productivity growth is reasonably strong right now but hasn't broken out, suggesting AI's promise remains further in the future.

As Nick Timiraos of The Wall Street Journal reports, "Warsh's remarks repeatedly cast AI as a question of national power, a theme upon which Fed chairs haven't typically dwelled. He recalled the late economist Robert Mundell calling America's rise as a superpower the most important fact of the 20th century, and said for the U.S. today, 'it is a charge to keep.'"

Focused on the bigger picture, Warsh offered no commentary on recent price action, the short-term trajectory of inflation or the Fed's current stance on interest rates .

As the dust settles on the midterm elections, Congress returns its attention to legislating. The GOP is left with only a few more weeks in charge before handing control over to the Democrats in January. The Republicans’ to-do list for this “lame-duck” period is evolving, but they won’t have time for everything. 

Priority number one is securing government funding, which expires December 11, to avoid a shutdown . Republicans are eager to act while they’re in power, but Democrats will demand concessions, like action on the Iran war. As a result, the odds of a shutdown have increased, although a deal remains possible. 

Second is an annual defense policy bill, the must-pass National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), which also sets the Pentagon’s budget for the year. Congress normally passes the NDAA without fail. It will likely do so again this year, though negotiations will be messy and require compromises by both parties. The biggest sticking point: Iran war funding, which could derail either of the must-pass bills. Dems will push for a provision to cut off the money. GOPers may thwart the effort, possibly by putting the funding into a…

items.title: Here's How to Prepare for a Bank Outage
items.summary:
The Associated Press reports that customers of Chase, U.S. Bank, and Wells Fargo have experienced service disruptions. Customers began encountering issues this morning, with more customers being impacted by early afternoon. 

A Chase spokesperson informed the AP that technical issues caused some transactions to take longer than usual, but customers have access to their accounts and money. Meanwhile, CBS News reported that Truist and Capital One customers also faced difficulties accessing their online accounts.

Coming on the heels of major outages with Microsoft Outlook and Teams, as well as the FAA grounding flights for hours on Friday, tech has had a challenging week. 

Outages can occur unexpectedly and typically last only a few hours. However, being unable to access your funds when needed highlights the importance of preparing for bank outages in advance. Here are several proactive steps you can take.

What to do if your bank is down right now If you're experiencing a bank outage, check your bank's official website or social media channels for service updates. You may still be able to access your money by visiting a local branch or using an ATM.

Avoid repeatedly submitting payments or transfers, as this could result in duplicate transactions once services are restored. Keep a record of any failed transactions and fees incurred during the outage so you can follow up with your bank.

Finally, be on the lookout for scammers posing as bank representatives. Never share your login credentials or security codes with someone who contacts you claiming they can restore access…
items.t: When Tech Fails Your Bank: What to Do When Chase Goes Offline

items.title: A Year-End Review Can Align Your Investments, Taxes, Goals
items.summary:
At year-end, many investors review gains and look for ways to manage their tax bills. A more meaningful review also asks whether their investment strategy, account structure, charitable goals and future priorities remain aligned.

The goal isn't simply to reduce this year's taxes . It's to improve after-tax outcomes over time without losing sight of risk, liquidity, costs and long-term objectives.

That's why the most impactful financial planning strategies include tight coordination between bankers, financial advisers and tax professionals.

Start with after-tax returns Taxes matter, but they shouldn't dictate investment decisions. A tax-saving investment isn't necessarily a good investment, and avoiding a taxable gain shouldn't prevent a change that supports long-term goals.

Depending on an investor's goals, municipal bonds , exchange-traded funds (ETFs) , separately managed accounts that hold individual securities and other tax-managed strategies might help improve tax efficiency while supporting the portfolio's overall direction.

A more useful year-end question: Is my portfolio still positioned to meet my goals after taxes, fees and investment risk?

items.title: We Have Generous Pensions. Do We Still Need Retirement Savings?
items.summary:
Dear Wealth Wise: My husband and I are both teachers in our late 40s. We're eligible to retire in our mid-to-late 50s and collect a full pension of a little more than 50% of our salaries, plus state-paid health benefits. We're also eligible for Social Security in our 60s. We haven't saved for retirement, given all this. We want to stop teaching as soon as we can get our full pensions and work part-time somewhere for a few years until we turn 65. Is this a good plan, or should we start contributing to our 403(b)s? 

While many private-sector workers would love the stability of pensions, they're a rarity these days. Only 14% of private-sector workers have access to a traditional defined benefit plan, according to a March 2026 Bureau of Labor Statistics report . 

By contrast, 86% of state and local government workers have access to a pension . That can take some of the pressure off retirement planning. 

Here, we have a couple who work as teachers and are eligible for a generous pension. They haven't specified the estimated monthly benefit they expect, but the median state and local government pension was $2,078 in 2024, the most recent data available. That would leave them with over $4,100 a month in today's dollars — an enviable amount of guaranteed income. 

Will the promise of steady income for life let them off the hook when it comes to retirement savings ? Not so fast, our experts say. 

A pension is a foundation, not a substitute for retirement savings The guaranteed income a pension provides can make retirement seem less scary. But that doesn't mean workers with…
items.t: We Have Generous Pensions. Do We Still Need Retirement Savings?

items.title: Why You Need Estate Planning Before You Feel Wealthy
items.summary:
Estate planning is often associated with families that have substantial fortunes, complicated trusts or an obvious tax issue. In practice, the need for deliberate estate planning can arise in families whose circumstances may appear far less complex at first glance.

A household can spend decades saving consistently, building retirement balances and watching a home appreciate without ever thinking of itself as particularly wealthy. Yet the financial picture may now include several types of assets, different beneficiary arrangements, a surviving spouse who will need flexibility, and children with different circumstances. 

The consequences of how those pieces fit together have become more significant, even if everyday life has changed very little.

The useful threshold is therefore not a particular net worth . It is the point at which ownership, liquidity and transfer decisions have become important enough that leaving them to default rules could produce an outcome the family didn't intend.

When your financial life becomes more complex than it feels Two households with similar net worth can have very different estate planning needs because the composition and purpose of their assets may be entirely different.

One family may hold most of its assets in liquid investments. Another may have substantial value concentrated in a home, real estate or a privately held business. 

One couple may expect to use most of what it has accumulated during retirement, while another places a high priority on leaving a legacy to children or grandchildren.

items.title: 5 Key Principles That Help You Build Financial Confidence
items.summary:
In my 42 years in financial services, one lesson has stood the test of time: Markets change, investment strategies come and go, and headlines shift daily, but human behavior around money remains remarkably consistent.

There is always a "next big thing" competing for attention, from dot-com stocks to cryptocurrencies to artificial intelligence. Through the noise, people want financial control, but many feel uncertain about whether they're making the right choices .

According to a new Financial Confidence report from Edelman Financial Engines (EFE), 84% of Americans prefer to stay actively engaged in retirement and savings decisions, yet only 40% of them know exactly how their 401(k) is invested. 

This disconnect between people's desire to take control of their financial future and their confidence in the decisions they're making is what EFE calls the Financial Confidence Gap.

This captures much of what I've seen throughout my career. People aren't looking for the next hot stock — they want reassurance they're making sound financial decisions. Helping people navigate uncertainty, whether that was Black Monday, the 2008 financial crisis or the pandemic, has defined the past four decades of my work.

Financial confidence doesn't come from guessing what the markets will do next. It comes from being prepared for whatever they do and knowing when to seek financial advice.

items.title: Is Selling the Family Heirloom Socially Acceptable?
items.summary:
Losing someone you care about brings profound sorrow, and when they leave you something valuable, the gift can make you feel conflicted. 

On one hand, you're thankful because it serves as a reminder of the fond memories you have of that loved one. On the other, what if you don't need what they left, and you could really benefit from selling it? 

This is a situation many people find themselves in and are unsure how to handle. Here's when it's socially acceptable to sell a family heirloom. 

When should I sell an heirloom? 

(Image credit: Getty Images) Richard Tilles , president of CIRCA, told Kiplinger that he sees people struggling with this all the time, and his advice is to keep it if it holds value or use it for yourself. It's going to be worth more to you than to potential buyers. 

However, he advises that if you don't have specific plans for the heirloom and it will sit around or get lost, sell it. 

When looking for a place to sell the heirloom, Tilles recommends taking it for an estimate from three different buyers. Look for those with an established reputation. Doing this can help you fetch a better price. 

Which items are fetching higher and lower values right now? 

(Image credit: Getty Images) Gold is at a historical price, Tilles says. Clients are shocked at how much gold jewelry is worth. People selling nice pieces from the 1970s and 1980s are getting almost twice as much today as they would have a few years ago.

Meanwhile, some items have dropped in value. Diamond pins from the 1950s have cooled down. They still have value, but less than they did 15…
items.t: Is Selling the Family Heirloom Socially Acceptable?

items.title: 6 Signs It's the Right Time for a Roth Conversion
items.summary:
After years spent building a retirement fund, giving up hard-earned growth to tax can sting. Yet, that's precisely what happens when you begin taking withdrawals from tax-deferred accounts such as your traditional IRA or 401(k). 

If you're looking to shield your retirement distributions from tax, a Roth conversion may be just the ticket.

Roth conversions involve moving funds from a tax-deferred account into a Roth IRA. In addition to growing tax-free, money in a Roth account can be withdrawn on a tax-free basis after age 59½, provided your account has been open for at least five years. 

Those tax-free withdrawals are the carrot, but there's also a stick — you'll owe taxes on the converted amount in the year of the conversion. Depending on your income level, tax bracket and the size of the conversion, that tax bill can be steep. 

However, if you time it right, Roth conversions can deliver benefits for years to come. Here are six signs the timing may be favorable.

items.title: $2,400 Social Security Increase Proposed for Retirees: What to Know
items.summary:
The historic 2026 midterm elections aren't fully in the rearview mirror, but a proposal to increase Social Security benefits by at least $2,400 annually is already getting attention.

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) is pushing Congress to pass the Social Security Expansion Act, legislation he introduced in February of last year with Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and other lawmakers. 

The proposal would increase benefits, change how annual cost-of-living adjustments (COLAs) are calculated, and raise additional revenue by changing the taxes that fund Social Security.

The legislation comes as Social Security faces a growing funding shortfall. According to the 2026 Social Security Trustees Report, the retirement trust fund is projected to run out of reserves in 2032. At that point, incoming revenue would cover only 78% of scheduled retirement and survivor benefits unless Congress acts. 

Sanders, who says the legislation would keep the Social Security trust funds solvent for 75 years, is expected to chair the Senate Finance subcommittee on Social Security starting in January 2027. That's when Democrats take control of both the U.S. House of Representatives and the U.S. Senate.

But how would the legislation work, who would pay more taxes to make it happen, and can it even pass? Here's what you need to know.

items.title: I Spent Years Editing Kiplinger. Here’s the Best Retirement Advice I Actually Use.
items.summary:
As the author of this column, I'm sometimes asked for advice by people on the brink of retirement who are nervous about how their lives will unfold once they're out of their work routine. 

With the caveat that each individual has to chart his or her own course, I'm happy to share the wisdom I've gleaned from sources I've interviewed, readers I've heard from, retired friends and family members and my own experience during the nine years since I stepped down as editor of Kiplinger Personal Finance .

One key point has been hammered home to me more times than I can count: Remember that you aren't just retiring from something; you are retiring to something.

That might be easy for those of you who have a long-standing hobby or interest that you'd like to pursue, or something new you'd like to try. 

One of my friends, a retired nurse with a passion for gardening, took the opportunity to become certified as a master gardener. I have musically inclined friends who are taking lessons on the guitar, violin, piano, bassoon and drums. 

When I took my first river cruise , I discovered there is an entire world of what I've dubbed "serial voyagers" — travelers who have taken dozens of cruises , sometimes several in a single year. One woman I know wears a T-shirt emblazoned with "Eat, Sleep, Travel, Repeat."

items.title: 5 Things Your Adviser Should Be Doing But Likely Isn’t
items.summary:
Plenty of people have a financial adviser and assume that means their financial life is fully handled. Sometimes it is. 

But "I have an adviser" and "my adviser is doing the things that actually move the needle" are different statements, and the gap between them can be expensive. 

A lot of advisory relationships quietly narrow down to managing a portfolio and little else, when the highest-value work often lives outside the investment account entirely. 

Here are five things a good adviser should be doing that, in my experience, many don't.

1. Proactive tax planning, not just investment management This is the big one. Most people think of their adviser as the person who manages their investments, and many advisory relationships stop right there. 

But for someone with meaningful assets, the tax planning around those investments can matter as much as the investment selection itself. I'm talking about looking ahead at your tax picture across years, not just reacting at filing time: 

When Roth conversions might make sense How to sequence withdrawals to manage your bracket When to harvest losses How to keep income below the thresholds that raise Medicare premiums For 2026, those Medicare surcharge thresholds begin at $218,000 of modified adjusted gross income for a married couple filing jointly, and crossing one can raise your premiums for a year. 

An adviser who never raises any of these issues is leaving one of the most valuable levers untouched. Investment returns get the attention, but tax efficiency is often when real, controllable dollars are found or lost.

items.title: Saved $10M? Here Are the Huge RMDs the IRS Makes You Take Starting at Age 73
items.summary:
If you have a traditional 401(k) or IRA, required minimum distributions (RMDs) are a part of life. Starting at age 73, these mandatory annual withdrawals are how the IRS finally gets paid. The exact amount you must withdraw each year depends on your account balance, age and life expectancy.

You might think RMDs are manageable and are just a necessary part of having a 401(k) or IRA. But they can negatively impact your taxes, Medicare premiums, and Social Security benefits, especially if you have a lot saved in those tax-advantaged accounts. 

That's why it's important to know how much your annual RMDs will be — especially if your 401(k) or IRA balance tops $10 million. 

Why it pays to know how much your RMDs are 

(Image credit: Getty Images) There are many reasons savers with $10 million or more in their traditional 401(k)s and IRAs should know exactly how much their RMDs are each year. With $10 million, the withdrawals will be large, which creates all sorts of problems, including: 

Higher taxes. Because withdrawals are treated as ordinary income, your RMDs could push you into a higher income bracket. Medicare premium surcharge. If your RMD pushes your income over a certain level, you're charged an extra Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount ( IRMAA ). Social Security taxes. Your RMDs will easily push you over the IRS income threshold, triggering the full 85% tax on your Social Security benefits. How much are your RMDs on $10 million? The exact amount you should withdraw annually from $10 million saved depends on your age and life expectancy factor.

items.title: 6 Ways the Changes in Congress Could Impact Your Retirement
items.summary:
The 2026 midterm elections are over, though a few races have yet to be called. Now the question is: What happens next, and what could the shifts in Congress mean for your retirement? 

Washington is entering a period of divided government, with Democrats in control of Congress and a Republican presidential administration. That shift could influence the direction of tax policy, federal spending, Social Security and Medicare . It could also create uncertainty about what changes may, or may not, happen before the next presidential election.

You may be thinking: 

Will taxes increase? (You can request a free copy of my bestselling book on tax planning, which features my research and what I think will happen with taxes in the future.) Could Social Security benefits change? What could happen with Medicare premiums and healthcare costs? Should you be doing anything differently with your investments? These are important questions, but as the founder and CEO of Peak Retirement Planning , I believe there's one principle worth remembering: You don't have to predict what will happen in Washington to prepare for it.

Your retirement plan should be built around your goals, your income needs and the financial decisions within your control. Understanding the political landscape can help you prepare, but reacting to every headline is not a retirement strategy. As I always say, when in doubt, zoom out. 

Today, I'm breaking down six areas where the changes in Congress could make a difference and what you can do to keep your retirement plan on track.

items.title: 5 Secrets to Building a Happier Retirement
items.summary:
Wes Moss is the author of The Retire Sooner Method and a managing partner at Capital Investment Advisors . He spent years interviewing more than 1,200 Americans to find out once and for all what the secret to a happy retirement is. 

Here, he talks with Kiplinger about what he found out. 

KIPLINGER: For your new book, you surveyed more than 1,200 Americans ages 50 and up. How did you determine who were the happiest? 

MOSS : I asked 35 questions about everything from their investable assets to the activities that brought them joy and purpose , then categorized everyone based on their life satisfaction, from the least happy to the happiest. 

Five factors produced the highest probability of happiness: hitting what I call the money green zones, in terms of income and assets; boosting meaningful activities that bring you joy and purpose; building a community; mapping out your future with a written financial plan or life map; and prioritizing quality sleep.

How much wealth does it take to hit the money green zone, and are those levels really attainable for most Americans? 

In my survey, the people who had $1 million or more in liquid investable assets, excluding home equity, were well above the U.S. baseline for happiness. Those who had $100,000 to almost $1 million were a little above it. I know most of America is in that latter spot; it’s hard to get to $1 million.

If you do have a million bucks, you should be able to withdraw at least 4% a year , or $40,000. If you’re married and collecting $5,000 a month in Social Security , that’s another $60,000. Throw in maybe a…
items.t: 5 Secrets to Building a Happier Retirement

items.title: How Ready Are You for Retirement on a Scale of 1 to 10?
items.summary:
When we have introductory meetings with prospective clients, we ask them to rate themselves from one to 10 on our "Retirement Readiness Scale." 

People typically think they're ready for retirement because they've been carefully saving throughout their careers and have healthy nest eggs by the time they start a conversation with us. 

When we ask them to rate themselves, we explain that an eight or higher means, at minimum, you've put together a Social Security optimization strategy and built what we call a "money map" of all your financial accounts in order of planned withdrawal in retirement. 

After hearing that, many rate themselves lower and ask us for help to get to the top of the scale. 

These are three factors that could derail your retirement even if you've gotten ahead of the curve by having robust retirement savings. By understanding them, you can enhance your position on the Retirement Readiness Scale.

items.title: 4 Money Lessons to Learn From Financially Solo Adults
items.summary:
Life rarely follows a straight line. Divorce, widowhood, career changes and other major life events can quickly transform shared financial responsibilities into solo decision-making. 

Nearly half of U.S. adults (46%) are single, according to the U.S. Census Bureau, and many are managing their finances on their own.

To better understand this growing segment of the population, Ameriprise Financial commissioned Flying Solo: Navigating Financial Autonomy , a study exploring how more than 3,000 single, divorced and widowed Americans approach their finances. 

What we found was encouraging: Financially solo adults aren't just managing on their own, they're doing so with pride and intention. Eighty-five percent say they feel financially confident, while nine in 10 (91%) report a strong sense of accomplishment from managing their finances independently. 

Their experiences offer valuable lessons for anyone, regardless of their relationship status, looking to build confidence, prepare for uncertainty and strengthen their long-term financial security.

items.title: Nasdaq Drops Friday But Ends the Week Up: Stock Market Today
items.summary:
Stocks opened higher Friday after mixed inflation data, but turned lower on continued weakness in tech stocks . Still, the three main benchmarks closed with impressive weekly gains. Looking ahead, there's plenty on next week's docket to keep markets volatile, including Nvidia's ( NVDA ) first earnings report without Jensen Huang at the helm and the highly anticipated Anthropic IPO .

At the close, the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite was down 0.9% at 25,136 and the broader S&P 500 was off 0.4% at 7,561. The blue-chip Dow Jones Industrial Average finished up 0.1% at 52,347.

Ahead of the open, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said the Producer Price Index (PPI), which measures wholesale prices, rose 0.3% from September to October — lower than economists' 0.4% forecast. But PPI was up 6.5% year over year, the highest annual rate since November 2022.

Core PPI, which excludes volatile food and energy costs, rose 0.3% month over month, in line with expectations. However, core PPI's annual rate of 5% was the highest since January 2023.

"The good news is that producer price inflation cooled from September," says Chris Osmond , chief investment officer for Fifth Third Wealth Advisors. "The bad news is that it may not have cooled enough to give markets the rate relief they want." 

Indeed, rate-hike odds rose after this morning's PPI. According to CME Group FedWatch , futures traders are now pricing in a 90% probability the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates by a quarter-percentage point at its December meeting, up from 85% one day ago.

items.title: Microsoft Outage Scams Are Coming: What to Watch for
items.summary:
Yesterday, a Microsoft outage that took down Outlook, Teams and other critical tools disrupted work and daily life for millions. The major tech company is still working out the issues and, as of this writing, Microsoft 365 products for both business and consumers are still experiencing service degradation . 

The widespread disruption has not only made work difficult, it's left millions vulnerable to a flurry of scams targeting Microsoft users . 

Eric Hulse, Vice President of Research and Development at Command Zero , an AI Security Operations Center, has seen similar scams happen in previous outages. When CrowdStrike went down in 2024, for example, Hulse says the company's own team members were sent malware under the guise of software that would "fix" the issue.

As you await word on progress or next steps from Microsoft, it's important to be wary of some of the most common types of online scams that tend to pop up during and after widespread outages.

What kind of scams should you watch for after the Microsoft outage? When it comes to scams built around widespread events like this, fraudsters take advantage of what people are trying to do next, according to Eric Hulse. "They want to fix the problem, get back into their account, reach support or get compensated, and there's a fake version of each."

The common scams you might see include:

Lookalike websites designed to steal your password and other information Fake support websites Calls or emails requesting access to accounts Promises of refunds for those affected by the outage Phishing links for restoring affected…
items.t: Microsoft Outage Scams Are Coming: What to Watch for

US existing home sales hit a 16-year low in October as buyers were driven away by high mortgage rates and rising inflation, according to new data released on Wednesday.

Sales of already built units dropped to 3.75m in October, down by 8.8% from last year, the National Association of Realtors (NAR) reported. The median existing-home sales price increased slightly to $416,700. Declines in sales were seen in the midwest, south and west, though sales in the north-east held steady.

Discount store giant Family Dollar will pay $63m to settle claims by state and federal authorities that it frequently overcharged its customers for milk, diapers, batteries, toilet paper and other household goods.

The enforcement action announced on Thursday by the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and 17 states followed a Guardian investigation that revealed Family Dollar and its larger rival, Dollar General, frequently charged more at checkout than the prices listed on their shelves. Family Dollar failed at least 2,100 price inspections in 20 states from 2022 to late 2025, the Guardian found.
